label: Monocausal frameworks generally attract low-information populations; anti-Zionism fits this pattern by analogy with other populist single-villain models
Best explanation of the correlation between anti-Zionist intensity and low foreign-policy literacy is that ignorance precedes adoption, not the reverse

defeaters.description: Bidirectional causation / feedback loop: Even if unsophistication precedes initial adoption, anti-Zionism may then actively degrade analytical capacity by providing a totalizing lens that crowds out competing hypotheses. The correlation data cannot distinguish a one-way causal arrow from a reinforcing spiral. Once adopted, the framework may function as an epistemic trap — making it harder to encounter or integrate disconfirming information — meaning anti-Zionism could be both symptom AND cause simultaneously, undermining the thesis's clean causal directionality claim.

label: If anti-Zionism provides moral closure that attracts the already-unsophisticated, it is selecting for pre-existing deficits rather than creating new ones

Convergence: if unsophistication precedes adoption, adoption doesn't degrade good thinkers, and anti-Zionism functions as an attribution engine, then anti-Zionism is best understood as symptom rather than cause

defeaters.description: Sophisticated anti-Zionists as direct counterevidence: Significant numbers of geopolitically literate actors — area specialists, IR scholars, veteran diplomats, journalists with deep regional expertise — hold anti-Zionist positions arrived at through detailed analysis rather than ignorance. If anti-Zionism were primarily a symptom of unsophistication, we would not expect this population to exist at the scale it does. Their existence suggests the thesis overgeneralizes from the most visible (activist/populist) instantiations of anti-Zionism to the category as a whole, committing a composition fallacy.
